title: GRE Vocabulary: Learn It the Way It's Tested
summary: GRE Verbal lives or dies on vocabulary in context — here's how to build it fast and make it stick.

nodes.label: Spaced review
nodes.note: Revisit on a schedule so it sticks

chunks.heading: Learn roots, not just words
chunks.body: GRE words cluster around **Latin and Greek roots**. Learning one root unlocks a family: *bene-* (good) gives benefactor, benevolent, benign. This multiplies your coverage far faster than memorising isolated words.
chunks.realExample: Know 'loqu/loc = speak' and you can reason out loquacious (talkative), eloquent, circumlocution and grandiloquent — four GRE words from one root.
chunks.memoryHook: One root = a whole word family. Learn the root, earn the family.

chunks.heading: Always learn a word in a sentence
chunks.body: The test uses words **in context**, so learn them that way. A word paired with a vivid sentence is remembered far better than a dictionary definition — and it teaches you the **usage** Text Completion actually checks.
chunks.realExample: 'Cantankerous' as a bare word is forgettable; 'the cantankerous old man argued with everyone' gives you the meaning AND the feel of how it's used.
chunks.memoryHook: No naked definitions. Every new word rides in a sentence.

chunks.heading: Track connotation — positive or negative
chunks.body: Many Verbal questions hinge on whether a blank needs a **positive or negative** word. Tag each new word with its **charge** (+/−). Even if you're unsure of the exact meaning, the right charge often eliminates half the options.
chunks.realExample: In 'the critic's ___ review ended the play's run', the charge must be negative — 'scathing', not 'glowing'. Charge alone kills the wrong-direction traps.
chunks.memoryHook: Tag every word +, − or neutral. Charge alone eliminates half the traps.

chunks.heading: Review on a spaced schedule
chunks.body: Vocabulary fades without **spaced repetition** — revisit words at growing intervals (a day, three days, a week) so they move into long-term memory. A steady 15–20 words a day, reviewed, beats cramming hundreds once.
chunks.realExample: Use these Smart Note recall cards: finishing the quiz schedules the words for spaced review automatically, so they resurface right before you'd forget them.
chunks.memoryHook: Little and often, on a spacing schedule. Cramming vocab is forgetting vocab.

recall.q: Why learn Latin and Greek roots for the GRE?
recall.a: One root unlocks a whole family of words (e.g. loqu/loc → loquacious, eloquent), multiplying your coverage.

recall.q: Why learn each word inside a sentence?
recall.a: The GRE tests words in context, so learning usage sticks better and matches how Text Completion checks them.

recall.q: What does tagging a word's 'connotation' help you do?
recall.a: Knowing whether a blank needs a positive or negative word often eliminates half the options, even without the exact meaning.

recall.q: What's the most effective review schedule for vocabulary?
recall.a: Spaced repetition — revisit words at growing intervals so they enter long-term memory.

recall.q: Is it better to cram hundreds of words or do a steady daily set?
recall.a: A steady daily set (e.g. 15–20 words) with spaced review beats cramming hundreds at once.
